### Transcaval Access for Large-Bore Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

#### Introduction
Transcatheter structural heart and endovascular interventions have expanded rapidly over the past two decades. Procedures such as transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), mechanical circulatory support (MCS) with microaxial flow pumps, and endovascular aortic repair (EVAR/TEVAR) require large-bore arterial access, typically measuring 14-Fr to 24-Fr [1, 2]. Although the transfemoral approach is the gold standard, approximately 5% to 10% of patients present with severe peripheral arterial disease, calcification, or tortuosity that precludes its use [3, 4, 5]. Traditional surgical alternative routes, such as transapical, transaortic, or subclavian/transaxillary access, are invasive and carry significant morbidity, making percutaneous alternative pathways highly desirable [6, 7]. Transcaval (caval-aortic) access has emerged as a completely percutaneous, safe, and highly effective alternative route that bypasses hostile iliofemoral anatomy by traversing the wall of the abdominal aorta from the adjacent inferior vena cava (IVC) [1, 8].

#### Underlying Physiology and Concept
The physiology of transcaval access is inherently counterintuitive but highly robust. First validated in animal models [2] and translated to human application [1], the technique exploits pressure gradients in the retroperitoneum. While creating an intentional aortocaval connection would typically raise concerns about catastrophic hemorrhage, the surrounding retroperitoneal interstitial pressure exceeds the venous pressure in the IVC. Consequently, any blood leaking from the aortic puncture site decompresses directly into the low-pressure venous "sink" of the vena cava, preventing retroperitoneal hematoma formation [8, 9]. This unique hemodynamic decompression allows operators to introduce large-caliber sheaths and safely close the tract percutaneously [10].

#### Preprocedural CT Planning
Meticulous preprocedural evaluation using contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is the cornerstone of transcaval access [11, 12]. Planning requires identifying an optimal "calcium-free window" on the infrarenal abdominal aorta that directly abuts the adjacent IVC [12]. The target must avoid major branch vessels (such as renal, lumbar, or mesenteric arteries) and present minimal calcification to ensure a successful puncture and reliable closure [8, 12]. Extensive CT-based screening protocols are now standard to determine anatomic suitability and optimize procedural success [12].

#### Procedural Technique and Crossing
The procedure is conducted using standard interventional equipment. A target snare is deployed in the infrarenal aorta via femoral arterial access. From the femoral vein, a guiding catheter is advanced into the IVC and oriented towards the aortic target [8, 13]. Crossing is achieved electrosurgically by applying radiofrequency energy to a standard 0.014-inch guidewire, which vaporizes a micro-pathway through the adjacent vessel walls into the snare [8, 13]. Alternatively, laser-assisted crossing techniques can be utilized for resistant aortic walls [14]. Once the wire is snared and externalized, the track is dilated, allowing the large-bore delivery sheath to cross from the vein directly into the aorta, through which TAVR or MCS can be completed [1, 9, 15].

#### Aortocaval Closure Strategies
Upon completion of the intervention, the cavo-aortic tract must be closed to eliminate the residual fistula. The default approach involves deploying a nitinol cardiac occluder (such as the Amplatzer Ductal Occluder) off-label across the aortic and venous walls under fluoroscopic guidance [8, 9]. Long-term data indicate that these fistulas undergo spontaneous thrombosis and heal completely within 12 months in over 90% of cases, without late migration or vessel injury [10]. Dedicated percutaneous transcaval closure devices have also been designed and validated in first-in-human clinical testing, demonstrating rapid, complete tract closure [16]. In patients with prior surgical reconstructions, successful transcaval interventions have also been performed through synthetic polyester abdominal aortic grafts [17, 18].

#### Clinical Applications Beyond TAVR
Initially popularized for TAVR, transcaval access has proven highly versatile. In mechanical circulatory support, transcaval access facilitates the percutaneous delivery of high-flow microaxial pumps (such as the Impella 5.0) in patients with cardiogenic shock, avoiding the need for surgical axillary cutdown and mitigating distal limb ischemia [15, 19, 20]. It has also been used for temporary venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) circuit placement in emergent settings [21]. Furthermore, endovascular specialists utilize transcaval access to perform embolization of persistent type II endoleaks after EVAR, exploiting the direct path from the IVC into the expanding aneurysm sac [22, 23, 24], as well as for percutaneous thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) [25].

#### Clinical Outcomes and Meta-Analyses
A growing body of clinical evidence supports the efficacy and safety of the transcaval approach. Prominent registries, including a multicenter European registry [4] and large-scale propensity-weighted analyses from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology (STS/ACC) Transcatheter Valve Therapy (TVT) registry [26], demonstrate that transcaval access is non-inferior to other alternative routes. Specifically, transcaval TAVR is associated with a significantly lower rate of stroke and neurovascular complications compared to transaxillary access, with comparable bleeding risks and a higher rate of direct discharge to home [7, 26]. Single-center series have shown lower rates of acute kidney injury and shorter hospital stays when compared to surgical alternatives [5]. Multiple comprehensive meta-analyses have validated these findings, concluding that transcaval access is a safe, reproducible, and effective alternative pathway when transfemoral access is contraindicated [27, 28, 29].

#### Conclusion
Transcaval access has matured from a novel conceptual technique to an indispensable tool in the structural heart and endovascular arsenal. Adhering to the "7 pillars" of procedural execution—encompassing careful patient selection, precise electrosurgical crossing, and structured closure—ensures highly predictable outcomes [30]. As transcatheter interventions continue to expand to younger and more complex patient populations, standardized percutaneous alternative routes like transcaval access will remain critical to optimizing clinical outcomes and avoiding the invasiveness of open surgery [6, 8].
